name: Physical Chemistry
tagline: Thermodynamics, kinetics, and the laws governing molecular behavior.
seo_title: Physical Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Physical Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in thermodynamics, kinetics, quantum chemistry and spectroscopy.

definition.lead: Physical chemistry uses the laws of physics to explain why chemical change happens, how fast it goes and how much energy it involves.
definition.body: It answers three questions about any reaction: can it happen (thermodynamics), how fast will it go (kinetics), and why do molecules behave as they do (quantum mechanics). Batteries, spectra, industrial reaction rates and the colours of molecules are all understood through it.

facts.label: big questions: can it react, how fast, and why
the first journal of physical chemistry is founded by Ostwald and van 't Hoff
the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to a physical chemist, van 't Hoff

branches.name: Thermodynamics
branches.summary: Energy, heat and whether a process can happen on its own.
branches.example: Gibbs energy tells whether a reaction is spontaneous.

branches.name: Chemical kinetics
branches.summary: How fast reactions go and through which steps.
branches.example: The Arrhenius equation links reaction rate to temperature.

branches.name: Quantum chemistry
branches.summary: Electrons described by wavefunctions: bonding, orbitals and energies.
branches.example: Molecular orbital theory explains why liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet.

branches.name: Spectroscopy
branches.summary: Reading molecules through the light they absorb or emit.
branches.example: Infrared spectra reveal functional groups; NMR maps how atoms connect.

branches.name: Electrochemistry
branches.summary: Chemistry that produces or is driven by electric current.

branches.name: Statistical mechanics
branches.summary: The bridge between single molecules and bulk properties.
branches.example: Boltzmann's S = k ln W links entropy to molecular arrangements.

branches.name: Surface & colloid chemistry
branches.summary: What happens where two phases meet.
branches.example: Car exhaust catalysts work only at their surface.

branches.name: Solutions & equilibria
branches.summary: How substances dissolve and where reactions settle.
branches.example: Le Chatelier's principle predicts how equilibria respond to change.

timeline.title: Boyle's law
timeline.text: Robert Boyle shows that the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely related.
timeline.why: One of the first quantitative laws in chemistry.

timeline.title: The ideal gas law
timeline.text: Émile Clapeyron combines earlier gas laws into a single equation of state.
timeline.why: PV = nRT is still the first model of any gas.

timeline.title: Gibbs and chemical thermodynamics
timeline.text: Josiah Willard Gibbs begins publishing 'On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances'.
timeline.why: Introduced the free energy that predicts whether reactions go.

timeline.title: A journal for a new discipline
timeline.text: Wilhelm Ostwald and Jacobus van 't Hoff found the Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie.
timeline.why: Physical chemistry becomes a field of its own.

timeline.title: The Arrhenius equation
timeline.text: Svante Arrhenius links reaction rate to temperature through an activation energy.
timeline.why: Explains why heating speeds up almost every reaction.

timeline.title: Nernst's heat theorem
timeline.text: Walther Nernst formulates the theorem that becomes the third law of thermodynamics.
timeline.why: Made absolute entropies and equilibrium calculations possible.

timeline.title: The Schrödinger equation
timeline.text: Erwin Schrödinger publishes the wave equation for electrons.
timeline.why: The foundation of all quantum chemistry.

timeline.title: Transition state theory
timeline.text: Henry Eyring, and independently Evans and Polanyi, describe rates through the activated complex.
timeline.why: Connected reaction rates to molecular structure.

timeline.title: Watching fast reactions
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Eigen, Norrish and Porter for studying extremely fast chemical reactions.
timeline.why: Opened the microsecond and nanosecond world of chemistry.

timeline.title: Femtochemistry
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Ahmed Zewail for observing reactions on the femtosecond timescale.
timeline.why: Chemists could finally watch bonds break and form.

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔG < 0. What does that tell you?
quiz.explain: A negative ΔG means the reaction is thermodynamically favourable. It says nothing about speed: diamond turning into graphite is favourable but immeasurably slow.

quiz.q: Which equation links a rate constant to temperature?
quiz.explain: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT): a higher temperature gives more molecules enough energy to cross the barrier.

options: The activation energy of the pathway
The overall ΔG of the reaction
quiz.explain: A catalyst opens a lower-energy route for both directions, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged.

quiz.q: Which is the ideal gas law?
quiz.explain: Pressure × volume = moles × gas constant × temperature.

quiz.q: Why does liquid oxygen stick to a magnet?
quiz.explain: Molecular orbital theory puts two unpaired electrons in O₂'s π* orbitals, making it paramagnetic. A simple Lewis structure cannot explain this.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 10 min. What fraction is left after 30 min?
quiz.explain: 30 min is three half-lives: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

quiz.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium…
quiz.explain: The right side has fewer gas molecules (2 versus 4), so the system relieves pressure by forming ammonia (Le Chatelier).

quiz.q: Which law states that energy is conserved?
quiz.explain: Energy can change form but is never created or destroyed.

quiz.q: In any spontaneous process, the entropy of the universe…
quiz.explain: That is the second law of thermodynamics.

quiz.q: In infrared spectroscopy, absorbed light changes a molecule's…
quiz.explain: IR photons match the energies of bond stretching and bending.

quiz.q: Who received the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1901?
quiz.explain: Van 't Hoff, for chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure. Arrhenius won in 1903, Ostwald in 1909, Curie in 1911.

options: Watching bonds break and form in real time
quiz.explain: Laser pulses lasting femtoseconds (10⁻¹⁵ s) are fast enough to freeze atoms mid-reaction.
